messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Coast Guard
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 64

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Future Orientation: Talking about the future, Auditory (Sirens): Sirens
  Maladaptive Strategies: Magical Thinking: I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel
  Memory: Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once
  Negative Appraisals: Defective Self: There is something wrong with me as a person, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arun, at eighty years old, moves through his small, quiet house with the practiced economy of a man long accustomed to solitude. It has been five years since his wife, Meera, passed away, but the true hollowing out of his world began decades earlier, on a churning grey sea off the Oregon coast. For forty years, he served in the Coast Guard, a source of immense pride that now feels like a brand of shame. He cannot deliberately recall the full sequence of that day; when he tries, his mind meets a strange, resistant fog. Instead, the memory lives in him as a series of disconnected, violent snapshots. The shriek of the winch cable under strain, the icy sting of salt spray hitting his face, the sickening, hollow thud against the hull, and the wail of the medevac siren that seemed to cut right through the storm’s roar. When these fragments ambush him, they are not memories but a full sensory assault. He is back on the deck of the cutter, the vessel lurching beneath his feet, the freezing rain soaking his uniform, the metallic taste of fear in his mouth.

In the immediate aftermath, Arun developed a set of silent rules for managing the intrusion. He learned to sense the approach of a memory and would immediately try to push it from his mind, a mental shove that left him breathless. If that failed, he would tell himself a story: it was a chaotic rescue, a freak wave was to blame, the event was not as bad as the fragments made it seem. When the guilt still clawed at him, he would force himself to think only of positive things—Meera’s smile, the birth of his son, the taste of a perfect mango—a desperate and exhausting act of will. He had come to believe the event was not a tragic accident but a direct result of his own personal failing. A better man, a more vigilant guardsman, would have anticipated the swell. The incident happened, he was certain, because of the sort of person he was: fundamentally defective. This belief became the lens through which he saw the world, a place of hidden dangers he was ill-equipped to handle.

This pervasive sense of threat dictates the geography of his life. His son has tried to get him to join a senior group at a new community center, but Arun refuses. He avoids any unfamiliar place where he cannot immediately assess the risks and identify all the exits. Even in his own home, he occupies only one chair: a worn armchair in the corner of the living room, which offers a clear view of both the front door and the hallway. From this post, he remains on constant guard. Yet, this vigilance coexists with a strange recklessness. Some evenings, he takes long walks after dusk, striding along uneven sidewalks without a flashlight, a part of him almost daring a fall. It is a quiet form of risk-taking, a way of tempting a fate he feels he probably deserves.

His triggers are woven into the fabric of daily life. An ambulance screaming past his street can leave him trembling for an hour, the sound yanking a sensory fragment of the failed rescue into the present moment. His son’s attempts to get him to visit a coastal state park are met with sharp, uncharacteristic anger; the sight of waves crashing against rocks is unbearable, a direct portal to his greatest failure. Even discussions about the future feel perilous. When his granddaughter recently spoke excitedly about her plans for college, Arun felt a wave of panic and nausea. He could not connect with her hopefulness; it felt like a language he was no longer permitted to speak. He abruptly changed the subject, leaving her looking confused and hurt. It was the look on her face that finally broke through his defenses. He saw his private torment was no longer private; it was now casting a shadow on the people he loved most. Arun has come to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a fragile wish to stop being a source of pain for his family, terrified that the defectiveness he feels within himself is, and always will be, irreparable.
